In Indian winters, red rose is the flower of romance, perfect for date nights and celebrations. Bold, beautiful and eternal.
broom: Broom flower smells sweet, honeyed and intensely sunny, like golden gorse bushes on a hillside with a coconut-like warmth. The bright yellow flowers have a distinctive sweet-pea-meets-honey character. In perfumery it adds a sunny, golden sweetness to spring florals. In India, its sunny warmth suits pleasant weather. A cheerful, golden floral off the beaten path.
pear-blossom: Pear blossom smells fresh, white and delicately sweet with a crisp green apple-like freshness. The orchard blossom is lighter than apple blossom, with an airy, transparent quality. In perfumery it brings fresh, youthful brightness to spring florals. In India, its crisp freshness is lovely in spring before the heat arrives. A fresh-faced floral for clear spring days.
wild-rose: Wild rose, or dog rose, smells simpler and more natural than cultivated varieties, fresh, light and hedgerow-sweet with green, dewy character. It evokes countryside walks and untamed nature rather than grand gardens. In perfumery it brings an authentic, unmanicured rose to natural-style compositions. In India, its natural freshness suits daytime in pleasant weather. The rose for those who prefer meadows to manicured gardens.
tobacco-blossom: Tobacco blossom is the flower of the tobacco plant, smelling sweet, honeyed and softly narcotic with none of the smokiness of cured tobacco leaf. The pale pink flowers have a jasmine-like sweetness with warm depth. In perfumery it adds a sweet, honeyed floral warmth to tobacco-adjacent and oriental compositions. In Indian winters, its honeyed warmth is lovely in evening scents. A surprising floral that bridges flowers and tobacco beautifully.
black-rose: Black rose is perfumery's gothic fantasy, no truly black rose exists, but the concept evokes dark, velvety, mysterious rose with smoky, leathery or oud-like depths. It is rose stripped of innocence, all midnight petals and dark secrets. In perfumery it centres dark romantic orientals and avant-garde florals. In Indian winters, black rose is pure evening drama. For those who find regular rose too pretty, black rose offers beautiful darkness.
peach: Peach in perfumery smells juicy, velvety and sweetly succulent, like biting into a ripe peach with its fuzzy skin, sweet flesh and hint of almond kernel. The note is almost always a reconstruction, but a good peach accord is instantly recognisable. It brings a luscious, feminine sweetness to fruity florals and gourmand-adjacent scents. In India, peach's juicy sweetness is beloved in the pleasant months, feeling indulgent and cheerful. In high summer it can turn cloying, so look for versions balanced with green or citrus notes. A universally loved fruit note that smells like golden afternoons.
black-currant: Black currant, or cassis, smells dark, jammy and intensely fruity with a distinctive green, almost catty sharpness from its buds. The berry's scent is more complex than simple sweetness, tart, deep and slightly wild. In perfumery it adds a dark fruity richness to chypres, fruity orientals and modern niche compositions. The bud absolute is particularly prized. In India, black currant's dark fruitiness works well in winter evenings, when its jammy depth feels luxurious. In summer the tartness can shine in fresh-fruity blends. A sophisticated berry for those who find strawberry too simple.
pear: Pear in perfumery smells crisp, juicy and green-sweet, like a fresh conference pear with its delicate skin and watery flesh. The note is light, fresh and universally appealing, bringing a clean fruity brightness. It is a staple of fresh fruity-florals and modern feminine scents. In Indian weather, pear's crisp freshness is wonderful in summer, light enough for heat yet more interesting than plain citrus. It is inoffensive and office-safe. A reliable, cheerful fruit note that works in almost any fresh composition.
raspberry: Raspberry smells sweet, tart and vividly red, like fresh berries with their distinctive seedy tang and bright juiciness. In perfumery it brings a playful, vibrant fruitiness to fruity florals, gourmands and youthful compositions. Less serious than black currant, more exciting than strawberry. In India, raspberry's bright tartness is delightful in the pleasant months, feeling festive and fun. In summer heat, choose versions with fresh or green balances. A joyful berry that smells like summer parties.
apple: Apple in perfumery usually means a crisp, fresh red apple character, juicy, sweet and clean with green freshness. It brings an innocent, fresh fruitiness to fruity florals and casual fresh scents. Green apple variants add tartness. In India, apple's clean freshness is perfect for everyday summer wear, inoffensive and uplifting. It is the fruit note equivalent of a white t-shirt, goes with everything, always appropriate. A staple of fresh feminine perfumery worldwide.
plum: Plum smells rich, jammy and darkly sweet with a distinctive wine-like depth and velvety texture. In perfumery it brings opulent, almost boozy fruitiness to orientals, gourmands and rich fruity compositions. Mirabelle and other varieties offer lighter interpretations. In Indian winters, plum's jammy richness is luxurious in evening scents, unfolding beautifully in cool air. In summer it is strictly for nights. A fruit for those who like their sweetness with depth and drama.
pineapple: Pineapple in perfumery is the tropical fruit at its most regal, juicy, sweet and vibrant with a distinctive tangy brightness. Creed's Aventus made pineapple a symbol of modern masculine luxury, its smoky-pineapple opening is instantly recognisable. In perfumery it brings confident tropical sweetness to fresh, fruity and niche compositions. In Indian summers, pineapple's tropical character feels completely at home, it was practically made for this climate. The key is balance, enough smokiness or freshness to prevent it turning syrupy in heat. A statement fruit for bold personalities.
cassis: Cassis is the French term for black currant, and in perfumery it usually refers to the bud absolute with its intensely green, fruity, almost animalic character. It smells darker and more complex than the berry, with a striking green-blackcurrant duality. Classic French chypres use cassis bud for their signature fruity-green opening. In India, cassis's sophisticated darkness suits winter evenings and those who appreciate classic French perfumery. A note with genuine heritage and depth.
litchi: Litchi, or lychee, smells delicately sweet, rosy and exotic with a distinctive grape-rose-water character and juicy translucence. The Southeast Asian fruit brings an elegant, refined fruitiness to fresh florals and romantic compositions. It pairs famously with rose, creating the beloved rose-litchi accord. In India, where litchis are cherished in summer, this note feels like home, its delicate sweetness perfect for warm weather. It is light enough for heat yet distinctive enough to be memorable. An exotic fruit with timeless elegance.
apricot: Apricot smells soft, velvety and golden-sweet with a distinctive fuzzy warmth and hint of almond. Less juicy than peach, more honeyed and comforting. In perfumery it brings a gentle, sunny fruitiness to soft florals, gourmand-adjacent scents and comforting compositions. In India, apricot's soft warmth suits winter and pleasant evenings, feeling nurturing and calm. In summer it can feel heavy, so enjoy it in cooler months. A tender, comforting fruit.
red-berries: Red berries is a blended impression of strawberries, raspberries, red currants and their cousins, all bright red juiciness and sweet-tart vibrancy. When pyramids list red berries, expect a cheerful, juicy fruitiness rather than any single berry. In perfumery it brings playful, youthful energy to fruity florals and fun fresh scents. In India, red berry blends are delightful in the pleasant months, festive and bright. In summer, keep them fresh with citrus or green balances. Pure fruity joy.
melon: Melon in perfumery usually means a watery, fresh cantaloupe or honeydew character, juicy, light and cooling with green freshness. It was the defining note of 1990s aquatic florals, all watery refreshment. In perfumery it brings a light, hydrating fruitiness to fresh and aquatic compositions. In Indian summers, melon's watery coolness is genuinely refreshing, like drinking cold water. It is simple and clean rather than complex. A nostalgic fresh note that still works beautifully in heat.
green-apple: Green apple is the tart, crisp side of apple, all sharp green freshness and mouthwatering acidity with none of the mellow sweetness. In perfumery it brings a bracing, modern freshness to sporty scents, fresh fruity compositions and youthful fragrances. It smells energetic and clean. In Indian summers, green apple's tart crispness is wonderfully refreshing, cutting through heat with precision. It is more exciting than red apple, with real personality. The apple for those who like their freshness with bite.
fruity-notes: Fruity notes as a general term covers the blended impression of various fruits, juicy, sweet and vibrant without singling out any specific fruit. When pyramids list fruity notes, expect a cheerful, juicy character supporting the main composition. In perfumery it appears in fruity florals, playful fresh scents and youthful compositions. In India, fruity blends are crowd-pleasers for casual daytime wear in pleasant weather. In summer, ensure they have fresh balances. The universal language of juicy sweetness.
red-apple: Red apple is apple at its sweetest and most mellow, all juicy red skin, sweet flesh and comforting familiarity. Less tart than green apple, more rounded and approachable. In perfumery it brings a sweet, innocent fruitiness to comforting fresh scents and fruity florals. In India, red apple's gentle sweetness suits everyday wear in pleasant weather. In summer it is best in light compositions. Simple, sweet and universally liked.
passionfruit: Passionfruit smells intensely tropical, sweet-tart and exotic with a distinctive seedy, almost fizzy vibrancy. The fruit's dramatic flavour translates to an equally dramatic fragrance note. In perfumery it brings bold tropical excitement to fruity compositions and summer scents. In India, passionfruit's tropical character feels completely natural, it thrives in heat and humidity. A little goes a long way, its intensity can dominate. For tropical fruit lovers who want maximum impact.
blackberry: Blackberry smells dark, jammy and richly sweet with bramble depth and a hint of green leaf. More complex than raspberry, less tart than black currant. In perfumery it brings a dark, luscious fruitiness to fruity orientals and rich gourmand-adjacent scents. In Indian winters, blackberry's jammy darkness is wonderful in evening compositions. In summer, use in fresh balances. A berry with depth and mystery.
fig: Fig in perfumery splits into two personalities, the green, milky, leafy fig of Mediterranean summers and the ripe, jammy, honeyed fig of the fruit itself. Both are beloved. The green fig smells fresh and vegetal; the ripe fig smells sweet and creamy. In perfumery it stars in Mediterranean-inspired scents and creamy fruity compositions. In India, fig's versatility shines, green fig for summer days, ripe fig for winter evenings. A fruit of genuine sophistication.
mango: Mango, the king of fruits, smells in perfumery like its glorious self, juicy, tropical, honeyed and intensely sweet with a distinctive resinous depth. In India, where mango is not just a fruit but a season, a culture, a passion, mango notes carry enormous emotional weight. In perfumery it brings lush tropical sweetness to fruity and gourmand compositions. In Indian summers, mango scents are pure joy, they smell like the season itself. The challenge is avoiding synthetic sharpness in heat. Done well, mango perfume is happiness in a bottle.
strawberry: Strawberry smells sweet, jammy and cheerfully red, the most universally loved berry in perfumery. It brings a playful, youthful sweetness to fruity florals, gourmands and fun fresh scents. Rarely sophisticated, always delightful. In India, strawberry's cheerful sweetness suits casual daytime in pleasant weather. In summer heat it needs fresh balancing to avoid cloying. The berry of first perfumes and happy memories.
cherry: Cherry in perfumery ranges from bright, tart Morello cherry to dark, boozy black cherry with almond undertones. Tom Ford's Lost Cherry made it a symbol of playful seduction. It brings a juicy, slightly dangerous sweetness to fruity orientals and gourmand-adjacent scents. In Indian winters, dark cherry's boozy richness is captivating in evening wear. In summer, stick to tart cherry interpretations. A fruit that flirts.
watermelon: Watermelon smells watery, fresh and green-sweet, like the pale rind more than the red flesh, with a distinctive aquatic juiciness. In perfumery it is almost always built on calone, the molecule that smells of watermelon rind and sea breeze. It defined 1990s fresh perfumery. In Indian summers, watermelon-calone freshness is incredibly cooling and refreshing. Simple, clean and effective in heat. Nostalgic aquatic freshness.
pomegranate: Pomegranate smells juicy, tart and jewel-like, with ruby-red sweetness and a distinctive tannic depth from its seeds and rind. In India, where pomegranate (anar) is beloved, this note carries cultural familiarity. In perfumery it brings a sophisticated tart fruitiness to fresh and fruity compositions. In Indian weather, pomegranate's tart juiciness works well year-round, refreshing in summer, festive in winter. A jewel-toned fruit with ancient roots.
red-currant: Red currant smells bright, tart and jewel-like, lighter and fresher than black currant with a sparkling red fruitiness. In perfumery it brings a vivid, tangy brightness to fruity florals and fresh compositions. Less common than other berries, it offers distinctive character. In India, its tart sparkle is lovely in summer fresh scents. A bright, underappreciated berry.
nectarine: Nectarine is peach without the fuzz, smelling juicy, sweet and slightly tangier with smooth, velvety richness. In perfumery it offers a more refined, less rustic fruitiness than peach. It brings elegant juicy sweetness to fruity florals and sophisticated fresh scents. In India, nectarine's smooth sweetness suits pleasant weather beautifully. A polished stone fruit for refined tastes.
red-fruits: Red fruits is a blended impression of the red berry family, strawberries, raspberries, currants, cherries, all juicy red sweetness and vibrant tartness. When pyramids list red fruits, expect a cheerful, juicy fruitiness. In perfumery it brings playful energy to fruity florals and youthful scents. In India, red fruit blends are festive and fun for pleasant weather. In summer, balance with freshness. Fruity exuberance in a bottle.
davana: Davana is a uniquely Indian aromatic herb from the Artemisia family, smelling fruity, woody and balsamic with a distinctive apricot-strawberry-tea character unlike anything Western. Used in Ayurveda and Indian perfumery for centuries, it is one of India's great contributions to world fragrance. In perfumery it adds an exotic fruity-woody depth to orientals and niche compositions. In Indian weather, davana feels like home, its complex character blooming in warm air. A treasure of Indian perfumery that deserves global recognition.
white-peach: White peach is the more delicate, floral side of peach, smelling soft, juicy and refined with less of the fuzzy intensity. It has an elegant, almost white-floral quality alongside its fruitiness. In perfumery it brings a sophisticated, gentle fruitiness to refined florals and soft fresh scents. In India, white peach's delicate character suits pleasant weather and elegant daytime wear. In summer it is best in light compositions. Peach with pearls.
guava: Guava smells tropical, sweet and musky-floral with a distinctive exotic richness, the beloved fruit of Indian childhoods. Its fragrance is more complex than simple sweetness, with floral and musky undertones. In perfumery it brings lush tropical character to fruity compositions. In India, guava notes evoke powerful nostalgia, winter mornings with salted guava. In perfumery it works in warm weather when its tropical nature feels natural. A fruit that smells like memory.
fruits: Fruits as a general term indicates a blended fruity character without specifying which fruits, the universal impression of juicy sweetness. In perfumery it appears in fruity florals and playful compositions where the overall juicy effect matters more than botanical accuracy. In India, fruity blends are reliable crowd-pleasers for casual wear. Simple, sweet and cheerful.
granny-smith-apple: Granny Smith apple is the tartest, crispest apple, all sharp green acidity and mouthwatering crunch with none of the mellow sweetness. In perfumery it brings a bracing, modern freshness to sporty and fresh fruity scents. It smells energetic and clean. In Indian summers, its tart crispness is wonderfully refreshing, cutting through heat. The apple for those who like their freshness sharp and invigorating.
blueberry: Blueberry smells sweet, dusky and softly fruity with a distinctive powdery bloom and gentle tartness. Less bright than raspberry, more mysterious than strawberry. In perfumery it brings a soft, dusky fruitiness to fruity florals and gentle gourmands. In India, blueberry's soft character suits pleasant weather, a gentle fruity comfort. In summer it needs fresh support. A quiet, dusky berry.
dried-fruits: Dried fruits evoke concentrated sweetness, figs, dates, raisins, apricots dried in the sun, all honeyed depth and chewy richness. In perfumery they bring a warm, opulent fruitiness to orientals, ambers and winter gourmands. The drying concentrates sugars and adds caramelised complexity. In Indian winters, dried fruit notes are magnificent in rich evening scents, their honeyed depth glowing in cool air. Strictly for cool weather, they would overwhelm in heat. Liquid autumn.
kiwi: Kiwi smells green, tart and exotically fresh with a distinctive fuzzy-tropical character, sweet yet sharp. In perfumery it brings a modern, zesty freshness to fruity and fresh compositions. It was trendy in 2000s fresh scents. In Indian summers, kiwi's tart greenness is refreshing and distinctive. A fun, modern fruit that stands out from the berry crowd.
big-strawberry: Big strawberry emphasises strawberry at its most generous and jammy, oversized sweetness with intense red fruitiness. In perfumery it signals an unabashed, playful strawberry blast. In India, it suits youthful, fun fragrances for pleasant weather. In summer heat, use sparingly. Strawberry turned up to eleven.
wild-berries: Wild berries evoke untamed hedgerow fruits, blackberries, wild strawberries, sloes, with a natural, slightly tart complexity beyond cultivated berries. In perfumery they bring a natural, outdoorsy fruitiness to green-fruity and natural-style compositions. In India, their wild character suits those who prefer natural over polished. A walk through brambles in scent form.
cranberry: Cranberry smells tart, bright and jewel-red with distinctive astringency and festive character. In perfumery it brings a tart, sparkling fruitiness to fresh and festive compositions. In India, its tart brightness works well in winter and the festive season. A crisp, celebratory berry.
quince: Quince is an ancient fruit smelling of apple, pear and citrus with a distinctive floral-honeyed character and firm, aromatic flesh. It was prized in antiquity and remains a connoisseur's fruit. In perfumery it brings a refined, old-world fruitiness to niche compositions. In India, its antique charm suits those who appreciate heritage. A fruit from perfumery's deep history.
sour-cherry: Sour cherry, or Morello, is cherry at its tartest and most vibrant, bright red acidity with intense juiciness and none of the dark booziness. In perfumery it brings a sparkling, mouthwatering tartness to fruity compositions. In Indian summers, sour cherry's bright acidity is wonderfully refreshing. The cherry for those who like their fruit with bite and sparkle.
champagne: Champagne as a note captures the effervescent, yeasty, celebratory character of sparkling wine, bubbly, bright and festive with fruity lift. In perfumery it adds a sparkling, joyful quality to festive and fresh compositions. In India, champagne notes suit celebrations and the festive season. Pure effervescence and joy in scent form.
carambola-(star-fruit): Carambola, or star fruit, smells crisp, juicy and star-bright with a unique sweet-tart balance and tropical freshness. The striking star-shaped fruit brings exotic visual and olfactory appeal. In perfumery it offers a distinctive tropical freshness. In India, its exotic character feels at home. A conversation-starter fruit.
grapes: Grapes in perfumery usually mean a juicy, sweet wine-grape character, fresh and fruity with a hint of vineyard greenness. In perfumery they bring a juicy, natural sweetness to fruity compositions. In India, grape notes suit pleasant weather, fresh and cheerful. Simple vineyard joy.
wild-strawberry: Wild strawberry, or fraise des bois, is strawberry concentrated to its essence, tiny, intensely fragrant and far more complex than cultivated varieties. It smells sweeter, more floral and more perfumed. In perfumery it represents strawberry at its most refined and natural. In India, its delicate intensity suits pleasant weather. The connoisseur's strawberry.
dates: Dates smell honeyed, caramelised and richly sweet with deep, almost molasses-like warmth. In the Middle East and India, dates are treasured, and their scent in perfumery brings opulent, natural sweetness to oriental and gourmand compositions. In Indian winters, date notes glow warmly in rich evening scents. Natural caramel sweetness with ancient roots.
papaya: Papaya smells tropical, musky-sweet and creamy with a distinctive exotic richness. The beloved tropical fruit brings lush, sunny sweetness to fruity compositions. In India, papaya's tropical character is completely at home, thriving in heat and humidity. A sunny, generous tropical fruit.
sorbet: Sorbet as a note captures the icy, fruity, refreshing character of frozen fruit desserts, bright, cold and palate-cleansing. In perfumery it creates a cool, sparkling fruitiness perfect for summer. In Indian summers, sorbet notes are genuinely cooling in effect. Frozen fruit refreshment in scent form.
rose-hip: Rose hip is the fruit of the rose, smelling tart, fruity and rich in vitamin C with a distinctive tangy-rosy character. In perfumery it brings a tart, natural fruitiness with subtle rose connections. In India, its tart freshness suits pleasant weather. A rose's fruity secret.
banana: Banana in perfumery smells creamy, sweet and tropical with a distinctive soft fruitiness, more comforting than exciting. It appears in playful gourmands and tropical compositions. In India, banana's creamy sweetness is familiar and comforting. Best in small doses and cooler weather. Creamy tropical comfort.
exotic-fruits: Exotic fruits is a blended impression of tropical abundance, mango, passionfruit, guava and their kin in juicy harmony. In perfumery it signals lush, vacation-like tropical sweetness. In India, exotic fruit blends feel like home, thriving in the tropical climate. Sunshine and abundance in a bottle.
tropical-fruits: Tropical fruits captures the lush, juicy, sun-drenched character of the tropics, a medley of mango, pineapple, papaya and coconut. In perfumery it creates an instant holiday feeling. In India, tropical fruit scents are in their element, the climate completes them. Pure tropical escapism.
vanilla: Vanilla is perfumery's most beloved sweet note, warm, creamy and comforting with endless depth, from smoky Madagascar pods to bright Tahitian flowers. The orchid-derived spice is the backbone of orientals, gourmands and amber compositions worldwide. In India, vanilla's warm sweetness is cherished in winter, when it glows like golden light on cool evenings. In summer heat, heavy vanilla can cloy, so choose lighter vanilla-musk blends for warm weather. Universally loved, vanilla is the comfort food of fragrance, and its quality varies enormously from synthetic flatness to rich natural depth.
tonka-bean: Tonka bean smells like vanilla's sophisticated cousin, warm, sweet and hay-like with distinct notes of almond, cinnamon and dried tobacco. The wrinkled black beans from South America contain high levels of coumarin, giving them their characteristic sweet-herbaceous warmth. Tonka is the heart of fougere and oriental compositions, adding a comforting, slightly powdery sweetness. In Indian winters, tonka's warm embrace is wonderful in evening scents. In summer, it can feel heavy, so look for it in lighter doses. A cornerstone of classic masculine perfumery with timeless appeal.
vanille: Vanille is simply the French word for vanilla, and in pyramids it usually signals a French-style vanilla, often richer and more complex than generic vanilla notes. Expect the same warm, creamy sweetness with perhaps more depth and sophistication. In perfumery the French term often appears in luxury compositions. In Indian weather, vanille behaves like vanilla, winter-wonderful, summer-careful. The name promises a certain je ne sais quoi.
caramel: Caramel smells exactly like its delicious namesake, burnt sugar, buttery and golden with deep, comforting sweetness. In perfumery it brings a gourmand richness to sweet orientals, gourmands and playful feminine scents. It is unapologetically indulgent. In Indian winters, caramel's golden warmth is delightful in evening and festive scents. In summer heat it can become overwhelming, so save it for cool weather. Pure edible comfort.
honey: Honey in perfumery ranges from bright, floral honey to dark, animalic buckwheat honey with waxy, almost leathery depth. It brings a natural, golden sweetness that feels more alive than sugar. In perfumery it enriches orientals, chypres and gourmand-adjacent scents with warm complexity. In India, where honey has Ayurvedic significance, this note resonates deeply. In winter, honeyed scents glow beautifully. In summer, choose lighter honey-floral blends. Nature's golden sweetness.
coconut: Coconut smells creamy, tropical and sun-warmed with milky sweetness and a hint of exotic warmth. In perfumery it instantly evokes beaches, holidays and tropical luxury. It stars in summer fragrances, tropical gourmands and beach-inspired scents. In India, coconut is culturally ubiquitous, from Kerala's groves to festive sweets, making this note feel like home. In summer, coconut scents thrive, they were made for heat and humidity. The ultimate tropical comfort note.
almond: Almond in perfumery usually means sweet almond, smelling of marzipan, cherry kernels and soft nuttiness with powdery warmth. Bitter almond adds a sharper, more intense character. It brings a comforting, edible sweetness to gourmands, powdery florals and oriental compositions. In Indian winters, almond's warm nuttiness is lovely, evoking festive sweets and cosy evenings. In summer, keep it light. Comfort in nut form.
praline: Praline is caramelised hazelnut sweetness, nutty, buttery and deeply gourmand with roasted warmth. In perfumery it is pure indulgence, the scent of patisseries and celebration. It stars in gourmand compositions and sweet orientals. In Indian winters and festive seasons, praline's celebratory sweetness is perfect. In summer it is strictly for cool evenings. Edible luxury.
coffee: Coffee in perfumery smells rich, roasted and darkly aromatic, from bright espresso to deep Turkish coffee with chocolate undertones. It brings a bold, adult sweetness to gourmand orientals and modern niche compositions. In India, with its strong filter coffee culture, coffee notes resonate deeply. In winter, coffee scents are magnificent, warm and enveloping. In summer, they can feel heavy, so choose lighter coffee-floral blends. The scent of morning ritual elevated to art.
rum: Rum brings boozy, caramelised warmth to perfumery, dark sugar, oak barrels and tropical spice with intoxicating depth. In perfumery it adds a swashbuckling richness to oriental, tobacco and gourmand compositions. In Indian winters, rum's warm booziness is perfect for evening wear, unfolding like a fine drink. In summer, it is too heavy for day but can work on cool nights. Liquid warmth and adventure.
madagascar-vanilla: Madagascar vanilla, or Bourbon vanilla, is the world's finest vanilla, grown on the island's rich soil and cured to develop extraordinary depth, creamy, dark and complex with hints of dried fruit and spice. It represents vanilla at its absolute peak. In fine perfumery it marks luxury compositions. In Indian winters, Madagascar vanilla's profound warmth is the ultimate comfort. Worth every rupee for vanilla devotees.
cacao: Cacao is raw chocolate before sweetening, dark, bitter and complex with earthy depth and fruity undertones. In perfumery it brings a sophisticated chocolate character to gourmand orientals, less sweet than milk chocolate, more intriguing. In Indian winters, cacao's dark richness is wonderful in evening scents. In summer, it needs careful balancing. Chocolate for grown-ups.
licorice: Licorice root smells sweet, woody and distinctly anise-like with dark, rooty depth. In perfumery it adds an unusual sweet-herbaceous character to orientals and avant-garde compositions. It is polarising, people love or hate its distinctive flavour. In India, where mulethi is familiar in Ayurveda, licorice notes have cultural resonance. Best in cool weather when its sweetness can unfold. Distinctive and divisive.
milk: Milk as a note captures creamy, soft, comforting lactonic sweetness, like warm milk with honey. In perfumery it creates the softest, most comforting gourmand impressions. It appears in milky florals, soft orientals and comfort scents. In India, milk's nurturing associations run deep. In winter, milky scents are wonderfully cosy. In summer, keep them sheer. Pure comfort in scent form.
sugar: Sugar in perfumery is straightforward sweetness, the simple pleasure of crystalline sweetness without complexity. It amplifies gourmand compositions and adds youthful fun. In perfumery it is rarely subtle. In India, sugar notes suit festive occasions and youthful scents. In summer heat, sugary scents can cloy quickly, so apply lightly. Sweet simplicity.
bourbon-vanilla: Bourbon vanilla is vanilla from Madagascar and Reunion (formerly Bourbon Island), the gold standard of vanilla with exceptional creamy depth and complexity. The name denotes the highest quality. In fine perfumery it signals luxury vanilla compositions. In Indian winters, its profound warmth is unmatched. The vanilla by which all others are judged.
coumarin: Coumarin is the sweet, hay-like molecule found in tonka beans, smelling of new-mown hay, vanilla and almonds with warm, comforting character. It is the backbone of fougere perfumery. In perfumery it brings a sweet-herbaceous warmth to masculine classics and comforting compositions. In India, its warm sweetness suits winter evenings. The quiet hero of traditional masculine fragrance.
hazelnut: Hazelnut smells rich, buttery and nutty with roasted warmth and creamy depth. In perfumery it brings a delicious nutty gourmand character to sweet orientals and festive compositions. In Indian winters and festive seasons, hazelnut's roasted warmth is delightful. In summer, it is too rich for day. Nutty indulgence.
sweet-notes: Sweet notes is a general term for sugary, candy-like sweetness without specifying the source. In perfumery it indicates a sweet character supporting the main composition. In India, sweet scents are beloved for festive occasions. In summer heat, sweetness needs careful handling to avoid cloying. General gourmand sweetness.
dark-chocolate: Dark chocolate is chocolate at its most intense and sophisticated, bitter, complex and deeply aromatic with minimal sweetness. In perfumery it brings a grown-up, almost mysterious richness to gourmand orientals. In Indian winters, dark chocolate notes are magnificent in evening wear. In summer, strictly for nights. Intensity and elegance.
chocolate: Chocolate in perfumery captures the beloved sweet's comforting, indulgent character, from milky to dark. It brings a delicious gourmand warmth to sweet compositions. In India, chocolate notes are festive favourites, perfect for winter celebrations. In summer, they can overwhelm, so save for cool weather. Universal indulgence.
whipped-cream: Whipped cream smells light, airy and sweetly dairy, like the softest cloud of sweetness. In perfumery it creates the most delicate gourmand impressions, all softness and comfort. In India, its light sweetness suits those who find heavy gourmands too much. Best in cool weather. Sweetness at its softest.
beeswax: Beeswax smells warm, honeyed and slightly animalic with a soft, waxy richness and golden depth. In perfumery it adds a natural, comforting warmth to orientals, ambers and artisanal compositions. It has an old-world, apothecary charm. In India, where beeswax has traditional uses, this note feels authentically natural. In winter, beeswax's warm glow is lovely. Golden, waxy comfort.
cognac: Cognac brings refined boozy warmth to perfumery, oak-aged grape spirit with caramel, dried fruit and sophisticated depth. More elegant than rum, more complex than whiskey. In perfumery it enriches luxury orientals and tobacco compositions. In Indian winters, cognac's refined warmth is perfect for distinguished evening wear. Liquid sophistication.
cacao-pod: Cacao pod refers to the whole fruit containing cacao beans, smelling fruity, earthy and complex with both chocolate and tropical fruit aspects. In perfumery it offers a more natural, less processed chocolate character. In India, its exotic complexity suits adventurous palates. Best in cool weather. Chocolate in its natural state.
bitter-almond: Bitter almond smells intensely of marzipan, cherry kernels and cyanide-like sharpness, much more dramatic than sweet almond. In perfumery it adds a striking, almost dangerous sweetness to orientals and gourmands. In India, its intense character suits winter evenings. Use with confidence, it makes a statement.
coconut-milk: Coconut milk is coconut at its creamiest and softest, milky, tropical and comforting without the suntan-lotion edge. In perfumery it creates the gentlest tropical impressions. In India, coconut milk's soft tropicality is lovely year-round, familiar and soothing. Creamy island comfort.
marshmallow: Marshmallow smells soft, powdery-sweet and pillowy with vanilla-musk comfort. In perfumery it creates the softest gourmand impressions, all gentle sweetness. In India, its soft character suits those who find heavy gourmands too much. In winter, marshmallow's pillowy comfort is delightful. Sweetness as soft as clouds.
cotton-candy: Cotton candy is spun-sugar sweetness at its most playful, pink, airy and nostalgically sweet. In perfumery it brings youthful, fun sweetness to playful gourmands. In India, it suits festive occasions and youthful spirits. In summer heat, apply very lightly. Pure carnival joy.
vanilla-absolute: Vanilla absolute is the purest vanilla extract, dark, rich and intensely aromatic with unparalleled depth. It represents vanilla in its most concentrated, luxurious form. In fine perfumery it marks the highest quality vanilla compositions. In Indian winters, its profound richness is the ultimate vanilla experience. Vanilla perfected.
white-honey: White honey is the lightest, most delicate honey, floral, clean and subtly sweet without the dark animalic depths. In perfumery it brings a refined, gentle sweetness to fresh florals and soft orientals. In India, its delicate character works in more situations than dark honey. In summer, white honey's lightness is wearable. Honey at its most elegant.
whiskey: Whiskey brings smoky, oaky, caramelised warmth to perfumery with rugged character and vanilla-barrel sweetness. In perfumery it adds a bold, masculine richness to tobacco, leather and oriental compositions. In Indian winters, whiskey's smoky warmth is perfect for evening. In summer, strictly for nights. Rugged sophistication.
brown-sugar: Brown sugar smells deeper and more caramelised than white sugar, with molasses warmth and comforting depth. In perfumery it adds a rich, warm sweetness to gourmands and orientals. In India, its warm sweetness suits winter and festive occasions. In summer, use sparingly. Comforting caramelised warmth.
toffee: Toffee is buttery, caramelised sugar cooked to rich, chewy perfection, smelling deeply sweet with butterscotch warmth. In perfumery it brings indulgent, buttery sweetness to gourmand compositions. In Indian winters, toffee's buttery richness is delightful. In summer, too heavy for day. Buttery indulgence.
pistachio: Pistachio smells nutty, creamy and subtly sweet with a distinctive green-nut character unlike other nuts. It has become a trendy gourmand note. In perfumery it brings a modern, creamy nuttiness to contemporary gourmands. In India, where pista is beloved in desserts, this note resonates culturally. In winter, pistachio's creamy richness is wonderful. Trendy nutty luxury.
tahitian-vanilla: Tahitian vanilla is the floral, fruity, almost cherry-like vanilla variety, brighter and more exotic than Madagascar. It smells less creamy, more radiant with distinctive anisic-cherry facets. In perfumery it brings a luminous, exotic vanilla to fresh orientals and tropical compositions. In India, its bright character works better in warm weather than heavier vanillas. Vanilla with a tropical twist.
tonka: Tonka is shorthand for tonka bean, the warm, hay-like, almond-vanilla seed that anchors fougere and oriental perfumery. It smells comforting, sweet and slightly powdery with coumarin richness. In India, tonka's warm embrace suits winter evenings. A classic comfort note.
chestnut: Chestnut smells warm, nutty and roasted with autumnal comfort and earthy sweetness, like roasted chestnuts on a winter street. In perfumery it brings a cosy, seasonal nuttiness to winter gourmands. In India, its autumnal warmth suits the cooler months. In summer, too heavy. Autumn in nut form.
white-chocolate: White chocolate is cocoa butter sweetness without the cocoa, creamy, milky and delicately sweet. In perfumery it brings a soft, creamy gourmand character lighter than milk chocolate. In India, its gentle sweetness is more wearable than dark chocolate. In winter, white chocolate's creamy comfort is lovely. Gentle cocoa indulgence.
sugar-cane: Sugar cane smells green-sweet, fresh and natural with grassy sweetness unlike refined sugar. In perfumery it brings a natural, tropical sweetness to fresh gourmands. In India, where sugarcane is ubiquitous, this note feels authentically tropical. In summer, its fresh sweetness works well. Natural tropical sweetness.
black-vanilla-husk: Black vanilla husk refers to the dark, cured vanilla pods with intense, smoky-sweet character and almost leathery depth. In perfumery it represents vanilla at its darkest and most mysterious. In Indian winters, its smoky sweetness is captivating in evening scents. Vanilla's dark side.
coconut-nectar: Coconut nectar is the sweet sap from coconut blossoms, smelling delicately sweet, floral and tropical with light caramel notes. In perfumery it offers a refined, less obvious coconut sweetness. In India, its delicate tropicality is beautiful. A sophisticated take on coconut.
vanilla-bean: Vanilla bean is the whole cured pod, smelling intensely of vanilla with dark, complex, almost boozy depth. In perfumery it signals the most authentic vanilla experience. In Indian winters, vanilla bean's profound richness is the real thing. Vanilla in its purest form.
